source.filename: 2019-Long Shape Memory Alloy Tendonbased Soft Robotic Actuators and Implementation as a soft Gripper.pdf

actuation: Shape memory alloy (SMA) wire tendons (Flexinol LT, Dynalloy)
Joule heating / electric current actuation (0.95 A)
constitutive_assumptions: One-dimensional constitutive behavior of SMA wire based on Brinson thermoconstitutive model
Initial stress in the SMA wire is assumed to be zero (sigma_0 = 0)
Initial strain in the SMA wire is assumed to equal maximum recoverable strain (epsilon_0 = epsilon_L)
Phase transformation contribution tensor Omega is assumed equal to -E * epsilon_L
Thermoelastic coefficient Theta is assumed to be zero
Martensite is assumed fully detwinned during pre-straining and during elastic matrix recovery upon cooling (initial martensite fraction xi_0 = 1)
Actuation starts from a fully martensitic state (minimum martensite fraction xi_M = 1)
Linear elastic beam behavior for the polymeric matrix (PDMS) with defined Young's modulus, cross-sectional area, and moment of inertia
Pure bending strain distribution varying linearly with distance from the actuator neutral plane
Dimensionless SMA curve-fitting parameter C_A set to 10.3 from literature
control_variables: Actuator matrix length (100 mm) and width (25 mm) for uniform rectangular specimens
Thermal cycle timing during fatigue tests (1 s heating, 9 s cooling)
Matrix material and curing protocol (Sylgard-184 PDMS cured at 55 °C for 8 hours)
Silicone guide tube inner diameter (300 µm) for 203 µm diameter SMA wire
Ambient room conditions and starting configuration (straight/unactuated)
dependent_variables: Pulling displacement sustained before slip or grip release (mm)
Adaptive grasping capability across diverse object geometries and weights
Cyclic repeatability / retention of maximum and minimum bending angle over 100 cycles
Actuator out-of-plane twist/torsion during asymmetric tendon actuation

evidence_relevant_to_topic.claim: Decoupling the length of the polymeric matrix from the SMA wire by using free-sliding tendons through silicone tubes enables large increases in bending angle (up to 400 degrees) and tip force (up to 0.89 N).
A quasi-static mechanical model coupling beam strain mechanics with Brinson's 1D SMA constitutive model accurately predicts bending angle as a function of tendon length up to physical contact limits.
Uneven tendon lengths on either side of the U-shaped routing produce pure planar bending without torsion due to tension distribution through free sliding in the silicone sleeve.
Modular finger packaging with V-shaped bearings routes 300 mm tendons compactly and withstands 100 continuous thermal cycles without degradation of maximum bending angle.
Three-fingered antagonistic and triangular soft grippers adaptively grasp diverse objects weighing from 5 g up to 1.5 kg (and withstand a 2 kg test weight).
The soft gripper achieves maximum pulling forces of 25 N in point contact and 30 N in power grasp using 0.305 mm SMA wires, maintaining high force over 40 mm displacement.
Wrapping actuator fingers in a low-friction TPU-coated sleeve drops maximum pulling force from 25-30 N to 7-13 N, demonstrating the critical role of interfacial friction in load capacity.
The modular soft gripper can be integrated as an end-effector on a commercial 6-DOF industrial robot arm (UR10) to execute pick-and-place tasks on real-world objects.

experimental_setup: Actuator fabrication: 203 µm Flexinol LT SMA wire placed inside 300 µm inner-diameter silicone tubing routed in a U-shape within a 3D-printed ABS mold, cast in Sylgard-184 PDMS, and cured at 55 °C for 8 hours

Bending angle characterization jig: Clamped actuator base with adjustable external fixation points (0 to 350 mm tendon length) for 3 mm, 5 mm, and 8 mm thick specimens, plus a tapered specimen (5 mm to 2.5 mm thickness, 680 mm tendon length)
Tip force characterization jig: Adjustable-angle guide jig with a Da Cell CB1-600gf load cell measuring tip force in 30° increments up to 120°
Asymmetric tendon test setup: 5 mm thick actuator with one tendon fixed at 10 mm and the opposite tendon varied from 50 to 200 mm to monitor out-of-plane twist
Compact finger modules: 8 mm thick matrix with 300 mm tendon routed internally over V-shaped bearings
Cyclic test bench: Automated thermal cycling for 100 cycles (1 s heating at 0.95 A, 9 s passive cooling)

Adaptive grasping trials: Three-finger antagonistic and triangular configurations tested across 36 diverse everyday objects (5 g to 1513 g, plus a 2000 g block) in horizontal and vertical orientations

Pulling force tensile test bench: Cometech QC-506 tensile testing machine evaluating 0.203 mm and 0.305 mm wire diameters against elliptical prism, half-cylinder, and inverted triangular prism jigs, with and without TPU-coated polyester low-friction sleeves
Robotic arm deployment: Modular gripper mounted as end-effector on a Universal Robots UR10 manipulator performing pick-and-place of a 273 g can
future_work: Improving the gripper to produce faster actuation and stronger grasping forces for industrial applications
Investigating active cooling mechanisms for the tendons to prevent excessive heat accumulation in the matrix and module housing
Exploring alternative heating methods beyond Joule heating to enhance heating speed and energy efficiency for extremely long SMA wires
Optimizing polymeric matrix geometry and cross-sectional profile in tandem with long SMA tendons to further enhance performance
Redesigning the module to be more compact using stiffer materials, smaller bearings, and optimized tendon arrangements
Adapting the long-tendon architecture to other robotic devices, mechanisms, and medical tools
independent_variables: Tendon length (0 to 350 mm for uniform specimens; up to 680 mm for tapered specimen; 50 to 200 mm for uneven tendon tests)
Actuator matrix thickness (3 mm, 5 mm, 8 mm, and tapered 5 mm to 2.5 mm)
Tendon symmetry (even vs uneven tendon lengths)
SMA wire diameter (0.203 mm vs 0.305 mm)
Contact jig geometry in tensile tests (elliptical prism, half-cylinder, inverted triangular prism)
Surface friction condition (bare PDMS matrix vs low-friction TPU-coated polyester sleeve)
Gripper finger arrangement (three-finger antagonistic vs three-finger triangular)
Object geometry and mass (5 g to 1513 g everyday objects; 2000 g weight)
Bending angle during force measurement (0° to 120° in 30° increments)
limitations_inferred: The quasi-static mechanical model ignores dynamic inertial forces, rate-dependent viscoelastic effects of PDMS, frictional dissipation between sliding wire and silicone tube, and 3D contact mechanics during grasping
Actuation is entirely open-loop (constant current and duration), lacking closed-loop force, position, or temperature feedback control
Passive cooling (9 s cooling required for 1 s heating) severely limits actuation frequency to approximately 0.1 Hz
Routing long wires over mechanical V-shaped bearings introduces mechanical complexity, potential friction losses, and mechanical wear not present in monolithic soft actuators
limitations_stated_by_authors: Actuator bending deformation can be physically limited by the actuator contacting its own driving tendons, the mounting jig, or folding onto itself
Tip force measurement was restricted to a maximum angle of 120° due to physical space limitations for positioning the load cell
Heat accumulation inside the matrix during repeated cycling causes an increase in the minimum unactuated bending angle during cooling
Thinner actuators exhibit poorer tip force transmission compared to thicker actuators due to intermediate compliance between base and tip
High pulling forces rely heavily on friction; reducing surface friction drastically reduces pulling capacity
Increasing wire diameter, wire count, or tendon length escalates electrical power demands and increases risk of heat accumulation
Standard Joule heating may become speed- and efficiency-limited when scaling to extremely long SMA wire lengths
Actuation speed remains slower than pneumatic actuators, requiring further design refinements before competing in high-speed industrial environments
main_results: Decoupling wire length from matrix length enabled significant increases in bending angle: the 3 mm thick actuator produced 213° at 100 mm tendon length and reached its physical limit of 270° at 200 mm; 5 mm thick reached 143° at 100 mm and reached its physical limit at 350 mm; 8 mm thick achieved 75° at 100 mm and 168° at 350 mm
A tapered actuator (5 mm base to 2.5 mm tip) with a 680 mm tendon achieved a maximum bending angle of 400°, reported as the largest among surveyed SMA-based soft actuators
Actuator tip force reached up to 0.89 N at 0° and decreased nearly linearly with bending angle; thicker actuators maintained higher tip forces throughout the deformation range
Asymmetric tendon lengths produced purely planar bending without torsion because tension equalized across the sliding U-shaped loop in the silicone guide channel
Across 100 continuous thermal cycles, the modular actuator exhibited no degradation in peak bending angle, with only a minor offset in minimum uncooled angle due to heat accumulation

The antagonistic three-finger gripper successfully grasped objects weighing from 5 g to 1513 g (full 1.5 L bottle) in horizontal and vertical orientations, while the triangular gripper grasped objects including a 2 kg block

Tensile testing demonstrated pulling forces up to 25 N under point contact and up to 30 N under full adaptive power grasp with 0.305 mm wires, sustaining near-peak force through 40 mm displacement and holding grip until 60-72 mm displacement
Reducing contact friction with a TPU-coated sleeve lowered maximum pulling force from 25-30 N to 7 N (0.203 mm wire) and 13 N (0.305 mm wire) on the elliptical jig
The modular gripper mounted to a UR10 robotic arm successfully executed grasping, transport, and release of a 273 g beverage can
modeling_methods: Quasi-static beam bending equilibrium model equating SMA wire actuation stress with polymeric matrix bending resistance
Actuator center plane strain and SMA wire plane strain calculation using linear elastic cross-sectional beam properties (eccentricity, Young's modulus, cross-sectional area, and moment of inertia)
Geometric kinematic relation between matrix length, tendon length, actuator plane strain, and net SMA wire strain
Brinson one-dimensional thermoconstitutive model for SMA stress-strain-temperature behavior with cosine-based martensite fraction evolution during strain recovery
performance_metrics: Tip force as a function of bending angle (N)
Sustained displacement under tensile load before grip failure (mm)
Maximum payload capacity / gripped object weight (g and kg)
Actuation response time to reach full deformation (s)
Cyclic durability (number of cycles without degradation of maximum bending angle)
possible_gap_implications: Decoupling smart-material stroke from structural body length via low-friction sliding channels provides a generalizable design paradigm for overcoming intrinsic strain limits in 1D smart materials without sacrificing cross-sectional stiffness

However, scaling tendon length increases thermal mass and cooling latency under Joule heating, highlighting an unresolved trade-off between stroke magnification and cycle bandwidth in thermally driven soft robotics
The reliance on high interfacial friction for payload retention underscores the need for integrating active variable-friction surfaces or mechanical interlocks in tendon-driven soft grippers
paper.research_objective: To develop and evaluate soft robotic bending actuators and modular soft grippers utilizing long, free-sliding shape memory alloy (SMA) wire tendons routed through polymeric matrices to decouple wire stroke from matrix length, achieve compact mechanical packaging via pulley/bearing modules, and significantly enhance bending deformation and grasping forces.
paper.research_problem: In conventional SMA wire-based soft actuators, embedding the wire directly within the polymeric matrix restricts the active wire length to the matrix length. Because SMA wires have a small recoverable stroke (4-8%), this direct coupling imposes an intrinsic trade-off between bending angle and force, leading to poor grasping and deformation performance relative to other soft actuation technologies.
paper.robot_type: soft robotic actuators and soft gripper
paper.title: Long Shape Memory Alloy Tendon-based Soft Robotic Actuators and Implementation as a Soft Gripper
